'''Stephen Louis Adler''' (born November 30, 1939) is an American [[physicist]] specializing in [[elementary particles]] and [[field theory (physics)|field theory]]. He is currently professor emeritus in the school of natural sciences at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in Princeton, New Jersey.

== Biography ==
Adler was born in [[New York City]]. He received an [[Bachelor of Arts|A.B.]] degree at [[Harvard University]] in 1961, where he was a [[Putnam Fellow]] in 1959,<ref name="MMA">{{cite web|title=Putnam Competition Individual and Team Winners |url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/putnam-competition-individual-and-team-winners |publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]]|access-date=December 12, 2021}}</ref> and a [[Ph.D.]] from [[Princeton University]] in 1964. Adler completed his doctoral dissertation, titled ''High energy neutrino reactions and conservations hypotheses'', under the supervision of [[Sam Treiman]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/2081377|title=High energy neutrino reactions and conservations hypotheses|year=1964}}</ref> He is the son of Ruth and [[Irving Adler]], and older brother of [[Peggy Adler]].

Adler became a member of the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in 1966, becoming a full professor of [[theoretical physics]] in 1969, and was named "New Jersey Albert Einstein Professor" at the institute in 1979. He was elected a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1974, and a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1975.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780-2010: Chapter A|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterA.pdf|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|accessdate=6 April 2011}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/adler|title=Stephen L. Adler|website=Institute for Advanced Study|language=en|access-date=2019-08-07}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/stephen-l-adler-kvmumt/|title=Stephen L. Adler}}</ref>

He has won the [[Sakurai Prize|J. J. Sakurai Prize]] from the [[American Physical Society]] in 1988, and the [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)|Dirac Medal]] of the [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics]] in 1998, among other awards.

Adler's seminal papers on high energy [[neutrino]] processes, [[current algebra]], soft [[pion]] theorems,
[[Sum rules (Quantum Field Theory)|sum rules]], and [[Perturbation theory (quantum mechanics)|perturbation theory]] [[Anomaly (physics)|anomalies]] helped lay the foundations for the current [[Standard Model]] of elementary [[particle physics]].

In 2012, Adler contributed to a family venture when he wrote the foreword for his then 99-year-old father's 87th book, ''[[Solving the Riddle of Phyllotaxis|Solving the Riddle of Phyllotaxis: Why the Fibonacci Numbers and the Golden Ratio Occur on Plants]]''. The book's diagrams are by his sister Peggy.<ref>{{cite book| last=Adler|first=Irving|title=Solving the Riddle of Phyllotaxis: Why the Fibonacci Numbers and the Golden Ratio Occur On Plants|title-link= Solving the Riddle of Phyllotaxis}}</ref>

== Trace dynamics ==
In his book ''Quantum Theory as an Emergent Phenomenon'', published 2004, Adler presented his trace dynamics, a framework in which [[quantum field theory]] emerges from a matrix theory. In this matrix theory, particles are represented by non-commuting matrices, and the matrix elements of [[boson]]ic and [[fermion]]ic particles are ordinary [[complex number]]s and non-commuting [[Grassmann number]]s, respectively. Using the [[action principle]], a [[Lagrangian (field theory)|Lagrangian]] can be constructed from the [[trace (linear algebra)|trace]] of a polynomial function of these matrices, leading to [[Poisson bracket#Hamilton's equations of motion|Hamiltonian equations of motion]]. The construction of a [[statistical mechanics]] of these matrix models leads, so Adler says, to an "emergent effective complex quantum field theory".<ref>''Quantum Theory as an Emergent Phenomenon'': [http://www.cap.ca/brms/Reviews/Rev711_592.pdf Book review by Collin Carbno] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224082618/http://www.cap.ca/brms/Reviews/Rev711_592.pdf |date=2013-12-24 }}</ref><ref>See also the review of Adler's trace dynamics in Tejinder P. Singh: ''The connection between 'emergence of time from quantum gravity' and 'dynamical collapse of the wave-function in quantum mechanics{{'}}'', International Journal of Modern Physics D, vol.&nbsp;19, no.&nbsp;14 (2010), pp. 2265–2269, World Scientific Publishing Company, DOI 10.1142/S0218271810018335 ([http://db.worldscinet.com/ijmpd/19/1914/free-access/S0218271810018335.pdf full text]). Preprint: [https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.2682v2 arXiv:1005.2682v2] (submitted on 15 May 2010, version of 12 October 2010)</ref>

Adler's trace dynamics has been discussed in relation to the differential space theory of quantum systems by [[Norbert Wiener]] and Amand Siegel, to its variant by [[David Bohm]] and [[Jeffrey Bub]], and to modifications of the [[Schrödinger equation]] by additional terms such as the [[quantum potential]] term or stochastic terms, and to [[hidden variable theories]].<ref>Mark Davidson: ''Stochastic mechanics, trace dynamics, and differential space&nbsp;– a synthesis'', [https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0602211v2 arXiv:quant-ph/0602211], submitted 25 February 2006, version of 21 Mar 2006</ref>
